sections.h2: Where is Springfield, Oregon, and how does it relate to Eugene?
sections.html:
Springfield is a city in Lane County at the southern end of the Willamette Valley, and it forms the eastern half of the Eugene-Springfield metro area. Eugene lies to the west, with Interstate 5 as the main dividing line, and the McKenzie River forms the city's northern edge.

The city sits at about 476 feet and covers roughly 16 square miles. The 2020 census counted 61,851 residents, which made Springfield the ninth most populous city in Oregon and about 4.1 percent larger than in 2010. Of 24,764 households, 52.9 percent of occupied housing units were owner-occupied.

School and utility boundaries do not always match the city line. Some western parts of Springfield fall inside the Eugene School District 4J, so a buyer's school question can depend on the exact street.

sections.h2: How did Springfield get its start?
sections.html:
Springfield began as farmland settled in the late 1840s and took its name from a natural spring in a prairie. The Kalapuya people had lived in the valley first and used controlled burning to keep it open.

William Stevens claimed land in October 1847, and Elias and Mary Briggs arrived in 1848. Springfield School District No. 19 was formed in 1854, and the city incorporated on February 25, 1885.

Timber then shaped the town for much of the 20th century. Weyerhaeuser opened its Springfield complex in 1949, and its sawmill and plywood plants closed in the 1990s while the paper plant was downsized. The city has since diversified. Springfield Creamery, started by Chuck and Sue Kesey in 1960, is another local name, and Matt Groening has said he named the fictional town in The Simpsons after Springfield, Oregon.

sections.h2: What are the main employers in Springfield?
sections.html:
Health care and public employers lead Springfield's job list, with PeaceHealth the largest at about 3,500 employees in the city's 2018 report. These are older figures, so treat them as a guide to the mix and not as current counts.

Hazelnut orchards surround the city, and harvest takes place in October. Across the Eugene-Springfield metro, wood products and recreational vehicle manufacturing are the biggest industries, and the University of Oregon and Lane Community College are large public employers nearby.

sections.h2: What neighborhoods and schools are in Springfield?
sections.html:
Springfield recognizes seven neighborhood areas, and most of the city is in the Springfield School District. The district runs 15 elementary schools, four middle schools and four high schools, and Thurston High School and Springfield High School are the largest by enrollment.

  • Downtown, home to the Washburne Historic District
  • East Kelly Butte
  • East Main
  • Gateway
  • Glenwood and Glenwood Riverfront
  • Mid-Springfield
  • Q Street

The Washburne Historic District in Downtown has its own rules. The city's ADU process, for one, calls for a Type 2 application there. Sellers with a downtown house who plan changes should ask the planning desk first.

sections.h2: What is the weather in Springfield, and what does it do to a house?
sections.html:
Springfield has a warm-summer Mediterranean climate, with hot, dry summers and wet, mild winters, and no monthly average above 71.6 degrees. Nearby Eugene gives a good picture of the numbers, with about 40.8 inches of rain a year over the 1991 to 2020 period, most of it in November, December and January.

Snow is sporadic and the median seasonal total is zero, though a 1969 storm dropped 41.7 inches. The Eugene record high is 111 degrees, set June 27, 2021, and about 16 days a year reach 90.

For a house, the long damp season is the main factor. Roofs, gutters, crawlspaces and siding take the beating, and buyers' inspectors check them closely. The McKenzie and Willamette rivers are close, so check a parcel's flood mapping if it sits low.

sections.h2: Can I add or sell a house with an ADU in Springfield?
sections.html:
Springfield allows accessory dwelling units, and the city currently waives several fees for new ones. Through June 30, 2027, subject to annual review, the city waives transportation, stormwater and local wastewater system development charges for newly permitted ADUs.

  • Willamalane Park and Recreation District charges still apply, though it allows deferral.
  • Most ADUs use a Type 1 land use application. The Washburne Historic District or alternative design standards call for Type 2.
  • A building permit follows land use approval.
  • The city offers a free ready-build ADU plan that reduces plan review fees.
  • Oregon law (House Bill 2001) bars cities from requiring ADU parking.

An ADU can be an apartment in an existing home or garage, an addition, a freestanding cottage or a conversion of an existing dwelling under 800 square feet. If you inherited a house with an unpermitted second unit, call the Planner on Duty at 541-726-3753 before listing. The city's ADU page lists the steps.

The Springfield Utility Board supplies electric and water service in the city. Springfield's council amended the charter on June 24, 1949 to allow a city-owned electric system, and SUB served its first customers about a year later.

SUB grew by acquisition. After it bought the local PP&L assets in 1975, electric customers rose from 6,800 to more than 15,000 and water customers from 3,000 to 7,750. It added about 3,000 Rainbow Water District customers within city limits in 1992 and had taken over the McKenzie Highway Water District in the 1960s. The city's population is now above 61,000.

sections.h2: When are Lane County property taxes due on a Springfield home?
sections.html:
Lane County property taxes are due November 15, February 15 and May 15, and the due date moves to the next business day when the 15th falls on a weekend or holiday. A full payment by November 15 earns a 3 percent discount. Two-thirds paid by then earns 2 percent on that amount, and one-third earns nothing.

Late interest is 1.333 percent a month, or 16 percent a year. It starts December 16 for the first installment, February 16 for the second and May 16 for the third. Checks go to the Lane County Tax Collector, and the county accepts online payment by card, e-check, Google Pay and Apple Pay.

For 2025-2026, Lane County mailed statements for 182,937 accounts. Total levies of $746 million were about 3.49 percent above the prior year, and total taxable value rose 4.38 percent. Value appeals were open through December 31, 2025. See the county payment page.

sections.h2: What must a Springfield seller disclose?
sections.html: Oregon requires most sellers to give a property disclosure statement to each buyer who makes a written offer, and the buyer has five days after delivery to revoke. Exclusions in ORS 105.470 cover sales by personal representatives, trustees, conservators, guardians, financial institutions after foreclosure and government agencies, and those sellers complete only Section 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Springfield house as-is?
faqs.a: Yes. You still provide the Oregon disclosure statement unless an exclusion applies, and a cash buyer prices the house in its current condition.
